title: Spectral evolution of two-photon emission in microresonators
authors: Francesca Famà, Stefano Dello Russo, Stefano Giaccari, Salvatore Virzì, Lorenzo Lucia, Cecilia Clivati, Chiara Gionco, Mario Siciliani de Cumis, Stefano Condio, Erik Cerrato, Gianluca Bertaina, Alice Meda, Marco Gramegna, Marco Genovese, Filippo Levi, Ivo Pietro Degiovanni, Davide Calonico
abstract: High-Q silicon nitride microresonators are versatile sources for generating photon pairs via four-wave mixing. We investigate the spectral coherence of this process, tracking the transition from the spontaneous quantum regime to the onset of optical parametric oscillation. By combining time-correlation measurements with phase-sensitive measurements, we continuously monitor the emission linewidth as it evolves from a cavity-lifetime-limited linewidth toward the pump-linewidth scale. This characterization is essential for optimizing integrated sources for scalable quantum networks.
summary: This paper characterizes the spectral evolution of two-photon emission in high-Q microresonators as they approach an Optical Parametric Oscillator threshold. By combining time-correlation measurements with advanced theoretical modeling, the authors track how the photon pair linewidth narrows from a cavity-limited value toward the pump laser's natural linewidth. This comprehensive characterization is vital for engineering stable and scalable integrated quantum light sources.
main_problem: The study investigates how the spectral coherence of two-photon emission evolves as a nonlinear microresonator transitions from spontaneous quantum pair generation to an optical parametric oscillation (OPO) regime.
main_result: The linewidth is observed to evolve continuously, transitioning from a cavity-lifetime-limited scale in the low-power regime toward the pump-linewidth scale near OPO onset. Theoretical analysis confirms this transition using piecewise fitting functions based on detuning.
method: The work combines time-correlation measurements (probing $g^{(2)}$) and phase-sensitive techniques like heterodyne beating to characterize coherence, supplemented by advanced theoretical modeling using QuantumCumulants.
model_or_system: The physical platform is a high-Q silicon nitride microresonator where photon pairs are generated via third-order Four-Wave Mixing (FWM). The dynamics are modeled across regimes ranging from spontaneous quantum emission to coherent OPO, requiring analysis of first and second-order correlation functions.
key_observables: Emission linewidth evolution, first-order coherence function ($g^{(1)}(	au)$), second-order correlation function ($g^{(2)}$), and effective detuning ($\delta_{	ext{eff}}$).
important_parameters: Cavity lifetime ($\sim 3 	ext{ ns}$), pump-linewidth scale, OPO threshold, and the effective detuning $\delta_{	ext{eff}}(\omega_p)$.
main_assumptions: Correlation measurements ($g^{(2)}$) are assumed to follow Siegert relations below threshold but fail above it; theoretical models often rely on large-occupation/mean-field approximations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the experimental setup for pair generation and detuning measurement, alongside schematics detailing coincidence counting and interferometric measurements used to probe coherence functions across different power regimes.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from describing the physical system (FWM in $	ext{Si}_3	ext{N}_4$ resonators) to outlining multiple experimental techniques for measuring coherence ($g^{(1)}, g^{(2)}$). It then details theoretical modeling, showing how analytic solutions must switch between different functional forms depending on whether the system is oscillatory or overdamped relative to the OPO threshold.
why_interesting: This work provides a detailed roadmap for characterizing nonlinear quantum sources, which is crucial for developing integrated quantum network components. The ability to track spectral coherence across the spontaneous-to-coherent transition using multiple diagnostic tools (time correlation vs. phase measurement) is highly valuable for quantum optics research.

A continuous-wave pump laser is split: 95% is phase-modulated to create weak fourth-order sidebands for cavity monitoring, while the remaining 5% is amplified and filtered to drive photon-pair generation in the microresonator. Two optical circulators are used to route the counterpropagating beams through the microring and detection paths.
